question: Which of the following best describes the concept of a 'geriatric syndrome' as distinct from a conventional disease?

answers.text: A single-organ disease presenting with typical signs and symptoms in an elderly patient

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Geriatric syndromes are NOT single-organ conditions — they arise from multiple contributing deficits across organ systems.

answers.text: A multifactorial clinical presentation resulting from accumulated deficits across multiple organ systems, producing a common final pathway such as falls or delirium

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Geriatric syndromes (e.g., falls, delirium, incontinence, pressure ulcers) share this multifactorial, multi-system origin — unlike conventional disease-based diagnoses.

answers.text: Any disease that exclusively affects patients above 60 years of age

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Age-exclusive occurrence is not the defining feature. Geriatric syndromes are defined by their multifactorial, multi-system pathogenesis and common clinical presentations.

answers.text: A psychiatric condition presenting alongside a physical illness in the elderly

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While psychiatric comorbidity is common, geriatric syndromes are not defined by psychiatric presentation — they are defined by multifactorial pathogenesis producing functional decline.

overallFeedback.feedback: Geriatric syndromes (falls, delirium, incontinence, pressure ulcers) arise from cumulative deficits across multiple systems — this is what distinguishes them from single-organ diseases.
Well done. Recognising the multifactorial nature of geriatric syndromes is essential for the Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment approach.
